questions.question: A nurse on an acute medical-surgical unit receives change-of-shift report on four clients. Which client should the nurse assess FIRST?

options.text: A client with chronic heart failure who has 2+ bilateral ankle edema and dry cough.
A client who had a thyroidectomy 6 hours ago and has developed noisy, high-pitched inspiratory sounds.
A client with diabetes mellitus admitted for cellulitis whose morning blood glucose is 210 mg/dL.
A client 1 day post-laparoscopic appendectomy who rates incisional pain 7/10 and requests pain medication.

questions.rationale: Inspiratory stridor following thyroidectomy indicates acute laryngeal edema or bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve damage compromising the airway. This is an immediate life-threatening emergency requiring tracheostomy or emergency intubation. Ankle edema in chronic HF, hyperglycemia, and post-op pain are expected findings that can wait.
questions.hint: Apply the ABC framework (Airway > Breathing > Circulation). Which finding signals an impending total airway obstruction?

questions.question: A nurse is preparing to administer the morning dose of oral digoxin 0.25 mg to a client with heart failure. Which assessment finding requires the nurse to HOLD the medication and immediately notify the healthcare provider?

options.text: Blood pressure of 134/82 mmHg.
Serum potassium level of 3.1 mEq/L and visual complaints of yellowish halos around lights.
Apical heart rate of 74 beats per minute with regular rhythm.
Serum digoxin level of 0.8 ng/mL drawn 6 hours after previous dose.

questions.rationale: Hypokalemia (potassium < 3.5 mEq/L) dramatically potentiates digoxin toxicity because digoxin and potassium compete for the same Na+/K+ ATPase pump sites. Yellow-green halos around objects, nausea, and vomiting are classic early symptoms of digoxin toxicity. The nurse must hold the drug and notify the provider immediately.
questions.hint: Look for electrolyte disturbances that make the myocardium hypersensitive to digitalis toxicity, combined with classic sensory symptoms.

questions.question: The nurse is caring for a client with a T4 spinal cord injury who suddenly complains of a severe, pounding headache and nasal congestion. The monitor displays BP 218/112 mmHg and HR 52 bpm. What is the nurse’s IMMEDIATE action?

options.text: Administer the prescribed PRN sublingual nitroglycerin tablet immediately.
Elevate the head of the bed to 90 degrees (high-Fowler position) and lower the legs.
Palpate the abdomen to check for fecal impaction.
Check the Foley catheter drainage bag for total hourly urine volume.

questions.rationale: The client is experiencing Autonomic Dysreflexia, a hypertensive emergency in spinal cord injuries at or above T6. The FIRST nursing action is to raise the head of the bed to high-Fowler (90 degrees) to induce orthostatic blood pooling in the lower extremities, lowering intracranial pressure and systemic BP. Checking the Foley catheter for kinks or distension is the second action.
questions.hint: Think: What non-pharmacological positioning action immediately uses gravity to lower dangerous intracranial arterial pressure?

questions.question: A charge nurse is making assignments for a registered nurse (RN), a licensed practical nurse (LPN/LVN), and an unlicensed assistive personnel (UAP). Which task is MOST APPROPRIATE to assign to the LPN/LVN?

options.text: Developing the initial nursing care plan for a client admitted with acute pancreatitis.
Administering routine subcutaneous enoxaparin and oral medications to a stable client 2 days post-stroke.
Providing discharge instructions regarding wound care and insulin administration to a newly diagnosed diabetic.
Assessing the neurological status of an unstable client who suffered a head injury 2 hours ago.

questions.rationale: LPNs/LVNs can administer oral, subcutaneous, and intramuscular medications, monitor ongoing findings, and care for stable clients with predictable outcomes. Initial assessments, care plan development, discharge teaching, and caring for unstable clients require registered nurse (RN) judgment and cannot be delegated (remember: do not delegate what you can E-A-T: Evaluate, Assess, Teach).
questions.hint: Remember the delegation mnemonic: Do not delegate what you can E-A-T (Evaluate, Assess, Teach). Which task involves routine medication delivery to a stable client?

questions.question: A client diagnosed with acute pancreatitis develops severe periumbilical bruising (Cullen’s sign) and involuntary muscle twitching of the face when the nurse taps anterior to the ear. What complication does the nurse suspect?

options.text: Retroperitoneal hemorrhage and acute hypocalcemia.
Splenic vein thrombosis and hyperkalemia.
Development of diabetic ketoacidosis and hypomagnesemia.
Hepatic encephalopathy and hypernatremia.

questions.rationale: Cullen’s sign (periumbilical ecchymosis) indicates severe retroperitoneal hemorrhage from pancreatic necrosis. Chvostek’s sign (facial muscle spasm upon tapping the facial nerve) signifies acute hypocalcemia, caused by enzymatic fat saponification in acute pancreatitis. Both findings represent severe disease progression.
questions.hint: Connect periumbilical ecchymosis with intra-abdominal bleeding, and facial twitching with calcium binding to necrotic mesenteric fat.

questions.question: A laboring client at 39 weeks gestation has an external fetal monitor in place. The nurse notes fetal heart rate decelerations that begin after the peak of the uterine contraction and return to baseline well after the contraction ends. What is the nurse’s PRIORITY action?

options.text: Increase the rate of the primary intravenous oxytocin infusion.
Turn the client onto her left lateral side and administer oxygen at 8-10 L/min via non-rebreather mask.
Instruct the client to take deep breaths and push firmly during the next contraction.
Document the finding as a benign early deceleration caused by fetal head compression.

questions.rationale: Decelerations that begin after the contraction peak and recover after the contraction ends are Late Decelerations, caused by Uteroplacental Insufficiency (inadequate fetal oxygenation). Immediate priority actions: Stop oxytocin, reposition to left lateral side (relieves vena cava compression), administer 8-10 L O2 via non-rebreather mask, and increase IV fluid bolus.
questions.hint: Recall VEAL CHOP: Late decels = Placental insufficiency. What position relieves aortocaval compression and maximizes uterine blood flow?

questions.question: A client with a right femoral central venous catheter suddenly develops acute dyspnea, cyanosis, tachycardia, and a loud churning sound over the precordium during a dressing change. What is the nurse’s FIRST action?

options.text: Place the client in Trendelenburg position on the left side and administer 100% oxygen.
Position the client upright in high-Fowler position and start a rapid normal saline bolus.
Obtain an immediate 12-lead electrocardiogram and draw troponin levels.
Perform immediate chest compressions and call a code blue.

questions.rationale: The client is experiencing an Air Embolism, evidenced by sudden acute dyspnea, tachycardia, cyanosis, and the classic "mill-wheel" churning murmur over the precordium. The nurse must clamp the catheter immediately, place the client in Trendelenburg on the LEFT side (which traps the air bubble in the apex of the right ventricle, preventing entry into the pulmonary artery), and administer high-flow oxygen.
questions.hint: How does positioning on the left side in Trendelenburg physically trap air inside the right atrium and ventricle to prevent pulmonary vessel occlusion?

questions.question: A client receiving intravenous heparin for an acute deep vein thrombosis has an aPTT of 128 seconds (control 32 seconds) and reports dark red urine. What medication should the nurse anticipate administering?

options.text: Phytonadione (Vitamin K).
Protamine sulfate.
Flumazenil.
Aminocaproic acid.

questions.rationale: The client’s aPTT is critically prolonged (128 seconds is 4 times baseline; therapeutic target is 60-80 seconds / 1.5-2.5x control) and active hematuria is present. The specific antidote for heparin toxicity is Protamine Sulfate. Vitamin K is the antidote for warfarin.
questions.hint: Identify the specific chemical antidote that binds and neutralizes unfractionated heparin.

questions.question: Four clients arrive at the emergency department triage desk simultaneously. Which client must the triage nurse assign as the HIGHEST PRIORITY for immediate medical intervention?

options.text: A 6-year-old child with a barking cough and mild inspiratory stridor whose SpO2 is 96%.
A 45-year-old with a compound fracture of the right tibia with palpable distal pulses.
A 28-year-old with acute asthma who was previously wheezing loudly and now has absent breath sounds ("silent chest") with lethargy.
A 72-year-old client reporting 8/10 epigastric burning pain relieved by liquid antacids.

questions.rationale: In severe asthma exacerbations, the sudden cessation of wheezing ("silent chest") combined with lethargy indicates complete respiratory muscle exhaustion and near-total airway occlusion. This client is in impending respiratory arrest and requires immediate endotracheal intubation. The compound fracture and croup child are serious but stable.
questions.hint: Be alert to the "silent chest" trap in asthma: when a patient who was wheezing stops wheezing, it is NOT improvement—it is respiratory failure.

questions.question: The nurse is caring for a client with active pulmonary tuberculosis. Which infection control measure is MANDATORY before the nurse enters the client’s hospital room?

options.text: Donning a sterile surgical mask and sterile gloves.
Donning a fitted N95 respirator mask and ensuring the room has negative airflow pressure.
Wearing a clean gown, eye goggles, and standard cloth face covering.
Placing a portable HEPA filtration unit directly outside the client’s open room door.

questions.rationale: Mycobacterium tuberculosis is transmitted via airborne droplet nuclei (<5 microns). Airborne Precautions require a negative-pressure isolation room with door closed (at least 6-12 air exchanges per hour) and healthcare personnel must wear a certified, fit-tested N95 respirator mask before entering.
questions.hint: Recall the airborne precaution diseases: MTV (Measles, Tuberculosis, Varicella). What specific mask and room pressure are required?

options.text: Signs of impending asphyxiation, such as acute change in vitals, dyspnea, or neurological status.
Mild chronic baseline discomfort that has been stable for several months.
Normal expected postoperative pain managed with oral analgesics.
A minor lab deviation within predictable parameters for this disease.

questions.rationale: In Anaphylaxis to IV Ceftriaxone, the development of acute physiological decompensation signaling asphyxiation requires immediate nursing intervention. Stable chronic symptoms and expected findings take lower priority.
questions.hint: Apply prioritization principles: Acute life-threatening signs of asphyxiation always take precedence over stable or expected baseline findings.

flashcards.back: Acetylcysteine (Mucomyst)
flashcards.notes: Prevents toxic metabolite NAPQI accumulation in liver; smells like rotten eggs; give within 8-10 hours.

flashcards.front: Emergency Antidote for: Opioids (Morphine, Fentanyl, Oxycodone)
flashcards.back: Naloxone (Narcan)
flashcards.notes: Opioid receptor antagonist. Shorter half-life than opioids: monitor for rebound respiratory depression.

flashcards.front: Emergency Antidote for: Benzodiazepines (Lorazepam, Diazepam, Alprazolam)
flashcards.back: Flumazenil (Romazicon)
flashcards.notes: GABA antagonist. Caution: can precipitate acute withdrawal seizures in chronic users.

flashcards.front: Emergency Antidote for: Heparin / Low Molecular Weight Heparin
flashcards.back: Protamine Sulfate
flashcards.notes: Positively charged protein that binds negatively charged heparin molecules to neutralize anticoagulant effect.

flashcards.back: Vitamin K (Phytonadione) / Kcentra
flashcards.notes: Promotes hepatic synthesis of clotting factors II, VII, IX, X. Takes 6-24 hours; use FFP for immediate reversal.

flashcards.back: Digoxin Immune Fab (DigiFab / Digibind)
flashcards.notes: Antigen-binding fragments that bind free digoxin molecules in life-threatening toxicity.

flashcards.back: Calcium Gluconate
flashcards.notes: Antagonizes neuromuscular blockade produced by magnesium toxicity (loss of DTRs, respiratory depression).

flashcards.back: Glucagon
flashcards.notes: Bypasses blocked beta-receptors by stimulating adenylate cyclase to increase myocardial contractility and heart rate.

flashcards.front: Emergency Antidote for: Calcium Channel Blockers
flashcards.back: IV Calcium Chloride / Calcium Gluconate & High-Dose Insulin
flashcards.notes: Overcomes calcium channel blockade to restore inotropic function.

flashcards.front: Emergency Antidote for: Cholinergic Crisis / Organophosphates
flashcards.back: Atropine Sulfate & Pralidoxime (2-PAM)
flashcards.notes: Competitively blocks acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors; 2-PAM reactivates acetylcholinesterase.

flashcards.front: Emergency Antidote for: Anticholinergic Toxicity (Atropine, Scopolamine)
flashcards.back: Physostigmine
flashcards.notes: Reversible acetylcholinesterase inhibitor that crosses the blood-brain barrier.

flashcards.back: Deferoxamine (Desferal)
flashcards.notes: Chelates free iron; turns urine vin-rose (reddish) color.

flashcards.back: Succimer (DMSA) or Dimercaprol (BAL)
flashcards.notes: Heavy metal chelating agent for pediatric lead encephalopathy.

flashcards.front: Emergency Antidote for: Ethylene Glycol / Methanol Toxicity
flashcards.back: Fomepizole or Ethanol
flashcards.notes: Competitively inhibits alcohol dehydrogenase, preventing conversion into toxic glycolic/oxalic acids.

flashcards.back: Hydroxocobalamin (Cyanokit)
flashcards.notes: Binds cyanide ions to form cyanocobalamin (Vitamin B12), which is safely excreted in urine.
Toxicity > 2.0. Hypokalemia increases toxicity risk. S/S: visual halos, nausea, bradycardia.
Toxicity > 1.5. Maintain normal sodium and hydration. S/S: coarse hand tremors, ataxia, polyuria.

flashcards.back: 10 - 20 mcg/mL
flashcards.notes: Toxicity > 20. S/S: horizontal nystagmus, ataxia, slurred speech. Causes gingival hyperplasia.

flashcards.back: 10 - 20 mcg/mL
flashcards.notes: Toxicity > 20. S/S: seizures, lethal tachyarrhythmias, severe vomiting.

flashcards.back: 10 - 20 mcg/mL (Severe: 15-20)
flashcards.notes: Draw trough 30 minutes before next scheduled dose. Nephrotoxic and ototoxic.

flashcards.back: < 2 mcg/mL
flashcards.notes: Draw trough immediately before next dose to prevent acute tubular necrosis and deafness.

flashcards.front: Therapeutic Level: Warfarin Target INR (Standard DVT/AFib)
flashcards.notes: Hold and contact provider if INR > 3.5 without bleeding; give Vitamin K if bleeding.

flashcards.front: Therapeutic Level: Warfarin Target INR (Mechanical Heart Valve)
flashcards.notes: Higher therapeutic range to prevent valve thrombosis.

flashcards.front: Therapeutic Level: Heparin Target Therapeutic aPTT
flashcards.back: 1.5 - 2.5x normal (60 - 80 seconds)
flashcards.notes: Normal un-anticoagulated aPTT is 30-40 seconds. Hold heparin if aPTT > 100 seconds.

flashcards.back: 4 - 12 mcg/mL
flashcards.notes: Monitor for agranulocytosis (fever, sore throat) and bone marrow suppression.
Crucial for cardiac conduction. Peaked T waves in hyperkalemia; U waves in hypokalemia.
Main extracellular cation. Neurological symptoms in hyponatremia (<135): seizures, cerebral edema.
Positive Trousseau / Chvostek signs in hypocalcemia. Bone pain and stones in hypercalcemia.
Low Mg causes Torsades de Pointes. High Mg depresses DTRs and respiratory effort.
Maintains osmotic pressure and acid-base balance.
Inversely proportional to Calcium. High in kidney failure.
< 7.35 = Acidosis; > 7.45 = Alkalosis.

flashcards.back: 35 - 45 mmHg
flashcards.notes: Respiratory parameter. > 45 = Respiratory Acidosis; < 35 = Respiratory Alkalosis.

flashcards.back: 22 - 26 mEq/L
flashcards.notes: Metabolic parameter. < 22 = Metabolic Acidosis; > 26 = Metabolic Alkalosis.

flashcards.back: 80 - 100 mmHg
flashcards.notes: Partial pressure of oxygen dissolved in arterial blood.

flashcards.front: Normal Lab Range: Blood Urea Nitrogen (BUN)
flashcards.back: 7 - 20 mg/dL
flashcards.notes: Evaluates renal clearance and hydration status.
Most reliable indicator of renal function.

flashcards.front: Normal Lab Range: Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR)
flashcards.notes: Stage 5 Chronic Kidney Disease (End-Stage) is GFR < 15 mL/min.

flashcards.front: Normal Lab Range: White Blood Cell Count (WBC)
flashcards.notes: Leukocytosis indicates infection/inflammation; Leukopenia indicates immunosuppression.

flashcards.front: Normal Lab Range: Absolute Neutrophil Count (ANC)
flashcards.notes: Severe neutropenia: ANC < 500 /mcL (requires strict protective isolation).
Thrombocytopenia: < 150,000. Bleeding precautions if < 50,000.
Oxygen carrying capacity of RBCs.
Lower threshold in pregnancy (> 11 g/dL in 1st/3rd trimester, > 10.5 in 2nd).
RBC volume percentage.
Elevated in dehydration; decreased in anemia and fluid overload.

flashcards.back: 11 - 13.5 seconds
flashcards.notes: Evaluates extrinsic coagulation pathway.

flashcards.back: 60 - 80 seconds (1.5 - 2x baseline)
flashcards.notes: Baseline aPTT is 30 - 40 seconds.

flashcards.front: Normal Lab Range: Fasting Blood Glucose
flashcards.notes: Diagnose diabetes if fasting >= 126 mg/dL.
Target in most diabetic clients is < 7.0%.
Major plasma protein maintaining intravascular oncotic pressure.

flashcards.front: Normal Lab Range: Total Serum Bilirubin
flashcards.notes: Elevated in liver disease, biliary obstruction, and hemolysis.

flashcards.front: Normal Lab Range: Newborn Total Bilirubin (Day 1)
flashcards.back: < 6.0 mg/dL
flashcards.notes: Phototherapy indicated if bilirubin rises > 5 mg/dL/day or exceeds 15-20 mg/dL.

flashcards.front: Normal Lab Range: Central Venous Pressure (CVP)
flashcards.back: 2 - 8 mmHg
flashcards.notes: < 2 indicates hypovolemia; > 8 indicates hypervolemia or heart failure.

flashcards.back: 5 - 15 mmHg
flashcards.notes: Pathological when sustained > 20 mmHg; treat immediately to prevent brain herniation.

flashcards.front: Normal Lab Range: Cerebral Perfusion Pressure (CPP)
flashcards.back: 60 - 80 mmHg
flashcards.notes: Calculated as MAP - ICP. Must remain >= 60 mmHg to ensure adequate brain oxygenation.

flashcards.back: ACE Inhibitors (Lisinopril, Enalapril)
flashcards.notes: Antihypertensive. Watch for dry cough, angioedema, and hyperkalemia.

flashcards.back: Angiotensin Receptor Blockers (Losartan, Valsartan)
flashcards.notes: Antihypertensive. Alternative to ACE-I if cough occurs; avoid in pregnancy.

flashcards.back: Beta-Blockers (Metoprolol, Atenolol, Carvedilol)
flashcards.notes: Hold if HR < 60 or SBP < 100. Bronchospasm risk in asthma.

flashcards.back: Calcium Channel Blockers (Amlodipine, Nifedipine)
flashcards.notes: Vasodilator. Causes peripheral edema and orthostatic dizziness.

flashcards.back: HMG-CoA Reductase Inhibitors (Atorvastatin, Simvastatin)
flashcards.notes: Cholesterol lowering. Watch for muscle pain (rhabdomyolysis) and liver toxicity.

flashcards.back: Proton Pump Inhibitors (Omeprazole, Pantoprazole)
flashcards.notes: Reduces gastric acid. Increases risk of C. diff and osteoporosis with prolonged use.

flashcards.back: H2 Receptor Antagonists (Famotidine, Ranitidine)
flashcards.notes: Reduces acid secretion. Safe for GERD and peptic ulcers.

flashcards.back: Penicillin Antibiotics (Amoxicillin, Piperacillin)
flashcards.notes: Cell wall inhibitor. High rate of allergic reactions; cross-reacts with cephalosporins.

flashcards.back: Cephalosporins (Cefazolin, Ceftriaxone)
flashcards.notes: Beta-lactam antibiotic. Avoid alcohol (disulfiram reaction with certain agents).

flashcards.back: Fluoroquinolones (Ciprofloxacin, Levofloxacin)
flashcards.notes: Broad spectrum. Black box warning: tendon rupture; increase fluids.

flashcards.back: Aminoglycosides (Gentamicin, Tobramycin)
flashcards.notes: Severe infections. Major ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity.

flashcards.back: Tetracyclines (Doxycycline, Tetracycline)
flashcards.notes: No milk/antacids. Causes tooth discoloration in kids < 8 and pregnant women.

flashcards.back: Antifungal (Fluconazole, Ketoconazole)
flashcards.notes: Treats fungal infections. Many CYP450 drug interactions; monitor liver enzymes.

flashcards.back: Antivirals (Acyclovir, Oseltamivir)
flashcards.notes: Treats herpes, shingles, influenza. Maintain high hydration with IV acyclovir.

flashcards.back: Beta-2 Agonists (Albuterol, Salmeterol)
flashcards.notes: Bronchodilators. Albuterol is rapid rescue; causes tremors and tachycardia.

flashcards.back: Methylxanthines (Theophylline, Aminophylline)
flashcards.notes: Bronchodilator. Narrow therapeutic window (10-20 mcg/mL); avoid caffeine.

flashcards.back: Corticosteroids (Prednisone, Dexamethasone)
flashcards.notes: Anti-inflammatory. Causes hyperglycemia, infection risk, osteoporosis; never stop abruptly.

flashcards.back: Low Molecular Weight Heparins (Enoxaparin, Dalteparin)
flashcards.notes: Subcutaneous anticoagulant in abdomen; do not expel air bubble; do not rub site.

flashcards.back: Direct Factor Xa Inhibitors (Apixaban, Rivaroxaban)
flashcards.notes: Oral anticoagulants for AFib and DVT; no routine INR blood checks required.

flashcards.back: Serotonin 5-HT1 Agonists (Sumatriptan, Zolmitriptan)
flashcards.notes: Acute migraine relief via cranial vasoconstriction; contraindicated in CAD and uncontrolled HTN.

flashcards.back: Thiazolidinediones (Pioglitazone, Rosiglitazone)
flashcards.notes: Type 2 Diabetes insulin sensitizer; contraindicated in heart failure (edema).

flashcards.back: DPP-4 Inhibitors (Sitagliptin, Saxagliptin)
flashcards.notes: Oral antidiabetic; stimulates insulin release; watch for pancreatitis.

flashcards.back: SGLT2 Inhibitors (Empagliflozin, Dapagliflozin)
flashcards.notes: Urine glucose excretion; causes UTI/fungal infections, euglycemic DKA.

flashcards.back: Bisphosphonates (Alendronate, Risedronate)
flashcards.notes: Treats osteoporosis. Take on empty stomach with full glass of water and sit upright for 30 minutes.

flashcards.back: PDE-5 Inhibitors (Sildenafil, Tadalafil)
flashcards.notes: Erectile dysfunction and pulmonary HTN. Strictly contraindicated with nitroglycerin.

flashcards.back: Look, Listen, Feel: Stridor, wheezing, tachypnea, cyanosis, and use of accessory muscles indicate immediate airway obstruction.
flashcards.notes: High-yield NCLEX clinical judgment knowledge point.

flashcards.front: Clinical Pearl: APGAR Scoring at 1 and 5 mins
flashcards.back: Appearance, Pulse, Grimace, Activity, Respiration (0-2 points each, max 10). Score 7-10 is normal; 4-6 moderate distress; 0-3 critical.
flashcards.notes: High-yield NCLEX clinical judgment knowledge point.

flashcards.back: Head 9%, Each Arm 9%, Chest 9%, Abdomen 9%, Upper Back 9%, Lower Back 9%, Each Leg 18%, Perineum 1%.
flashcards.notes: High-yield NCLEX clinical judgment knowledge point.

flashcards.front: Clinical Pearl: Parkland Burn Resuscitation Formula
flashcards.back: 4 mL x kg body weight x % TBSA burned. Infuse 50% in first 8 hours, remaining 50% over next 16 hours (from time of burn, not hospital arrival).
flashcards.notes: High-yield NCLEX clinical judgment knowledge point.

flashcards.back: Sensory: Smell identification in each nostril.
flashcards.notes: High-yield NCLEX clinical judgment knowledge point.

flashcards.back: Sensory: Visual acuity (Snellen chart) and visual fields.
flashcards.notes: High-yield NCLEX clinical judgment knowledge point.

flashcards.back: Motor: Pupil constriction and extraocular eye movements.
flashcards.notes: High-yield NCLEX clinical judgment knowledge point.

flashcards.back: Motor: Inferolateral eye movement (downward and inward).
flashcards.notes: High-yield NCLEX clinical judgment knowledge point.

flashcards.back: Both: Facial sensation and mastication (chewing).
flashcards.notes: High-yield NCLEX clinical judgment knowledge point.

flashcards.back: Motor: Lateral eye movement.
flashcards.notes: High-yield NCLEX clinical judgment knowledge point.

flashcards.back: Both: Facial expressions (smile, frown, puff cheeks) and anterior 2/3 taste.
flashcards.notes: High-yield NCLEX clinical judgment knowledge point.

flashcards.back: Sensory: Hearing acuity (whisper test) and balance.
flashcards.notes: High-yield NCLEX clinical judgment knowledge point.

flashcards.back: Both: Gag reflex, swallowing, and posterior 1/3 taste.
flashcards.notes: High-yield NCLEX clinical judgment knowledge point.

flashcards.back: Both: Uvula and soft palate elevation, parasympathetic control of heart/GI.
flashcards.notes: High-yield NCLEX clinical judgment knowledge point.

flashcards.back: Motor: Shoulder shrug (trapezius) and head turning against resistance (sternocleidomastoid).
flashcards.notes: High-yield NCLEX clinical judgment knowledge point.

flashcards.back: Motor: Tongue movement, symmetry, and speech.
flashcards.notes: High-yield NCLEX clinical judgment knowledge point.

flashcards.back: Measles, Tuberculosis, Varicella (Chickenpox / Disseminated Shingles). N95 respirator, negative pressure room with door closed.
flashcards.notes: High-yield NCLEX clinical judgment knowledge point.

flashcards.back: Influenza, Pertussis, Bacterial Meningitis, Mumps, Rubella. Surgical mask within 3-6 feet, private room.
flashcards.notes: High-yield NCLEX clinical judgment knowledge point.

flashcards.back: C. difficile, MRSA, VRE, Scabies. Gloves and gown before entering room, dedicated equipment, wash with soap & water for C. diff.
flashcards.notes: High-yield NCLEX clinical judgment knowledge point.

flashcards.front: Clinical Pearl: Blood Transfusion Reaction Protocol
flashcards.back: 1) STOP transfusion immediately. 2) Disconnect tubing at catheter hub. 3) Infuse Normal Saline with NEW tubing. 4) Notify provider and blood bank. 5) Send blood bag and urine sample to lab.
flashcards.notes: High-yield NCLEX clinical judgment knowledge point.

flashcards.back: Best for acute shortness of breath, respiratory distress, during and after NG feedings, and autonomic dysreflexia.
flashcards.notes: High-yield NCLEX clinical judgment knowledge point.

flashcards.front: Clinical Pearl: Positions: Trendelenburg (Head down, feet up)
flashcards.back: Historical for shock; used for central line insertion into internal jugular/subclavian and air embolism on left side.
flashcards.notes: High-yield NCLEX clinical judgment knowledge point.

flashcards.front: Clinical Pearl: Positions: Sims (Semi-prone on left side)
flashcards.back: Position of choice for enema administration and rectal temperature/medication administration.
flashcards.notes: High-yield NCLEX clinical judgment knowledge point.

flashcards.front: Clinical Pearl: Positions: Left Lateral Recumbent (Pregnant)
flashcards.back: Prevents supine hypotensive syndrome by shifting gravid uterus off inferior vena cava, maximizing placental perfusion.
flashcards.notes: High-yield NCLEX clinical judgment knowledge point.

flashcards.front: Clinical Pearl: Positions: Orthopneic (Tripod over bed table)
flashcards.back: Allows maximum chest and diaphragm expansion for clients with severe COPD, asthma, or orthopnea.
flashcards.notes: High-yield NCLEX clinical judgment knowledge point.

cheatSheet.title: Airway Compromise & Stridor
cheatSheet.meaning: Harsh, high-pitched vibratory sound caused by turbulent airflow through a partially obstructed extrathoracic airway. Indicates critical narrowing of larynx/trachea.
cheatSheet.detailedUsage: Immediately assess client respiratory effort and oxygen saturation. Prepare emergency endotracheal intubation or tracheostomy kit at bedside. Keep client calm and in high-Fowler position. Avoid inspecting throat with tongue blade in suspected epiglottitis.
cheatSheet.clinicalRule: Airway obstruction always trumps all other systemic, hemodynamic, or pain concerns.
cheatSheet.nclexAlert: Sudden cessation of stridor or wheezing in severe respiratory distress indicates complete airway collapse ("silent chest"), requiring immediate intubation.
examples: Post-thyroidectomy client with inspiratory stridor from recurrent laryngeal nerve damage or hematoma
Pediatric client in tripod position with drooling and stridor
cheatSheet.keyTakeaway: Airway patency is non-negotiable. Immediate intervention needed.

cheatSheet.title: Autonomic Dysreflexia (Hyperreflexia)
cheatSheet.meaning: Acute, uninhibited sympathetic discharge in individuals with spinal cord injury at or above T6 level, triggered by noxious stimuli below the lesion.
cheatSheet.detailedUsage: FIRST action: Elevate head of bed to high-Fowler (90 degrees) to induce orthostatic pooling. SECOND action: Check for bladder distension (kinked Foley catheter or need for in-and-out catheterization). THIRD action: Check for fecal impaction or tight restrictive clothing. Monitor BP every 2-5 minutes; administer hydralazine or nifedipine if BP remains critically elevated.
cheatSheet.clinicalRule: Sit upright immediately to lower intracranial pressure and blood pressure, then remove the offending noxious stimulus (Foley kink #1 cause).
cheatSheet.nclexAlert: Severe pounding headache, profuse diaphoresis above lesion, flushing, and severe hypertension with compensatory bradycardia.
examples: T4 spinal cord injury client with BP 210/110 mmHg, bradycardia HR 52, and profuse facial sweating
cheatSheet.keyTakeaway: Elevate HOB first -> check Foley -> check bowel -> loosen clothing.

cheatSheet.title: Anaphylaxis vs. Mild Allergic Reaction
cheatSheet.meaning: Type I hypersensitivity reaction involving multi-system mast cell degranulation leading to bronchospasm, laryngeal edema, and circulatory collapse.
cheatSheet.detailedUsage: First-line drug of choice is INTRAMUSCULAR Epinephrine (1:1,000) administered into anterolateral mid-thigh. Repeat every 5-15 minutes as needed. Supplemental high-flow O2 (100%), rapid IV fluid resuscitation (Normal Saline bolus), and secondary medications (IV diphenhydramine, methylprednisolone).
cheatSheet.clinicalRule: Never delay IM epinephrine for antihistamines or steroids. Epinephrine is the only medication that reverses airway edema and vasodilatory shock.
cheatSheet.nclexAlert: In an allergic reaction, if wheezing, stridor, hoarseness, or hypotension occurs, it is anaphylaxis: give IM Epi immediately.
examples: Client developing urticaria, throat tightness, and wheezing 5 minutes into IV penicillin infusion
cheatSheet.keyTakeaway: IM Epinephrine in mid-thigh immediately for airway involvement or hypotension.

cheatSheet.title: Tension Pneumothorax
cheatSheet.meaning: One-way valve leak trapping air in pleural space, compressing the ipsilateral lung, shifting mediastinum to contralateral side, and obstructing venous return.
cheatSheet.detailedUsage: Recognize triad of absent breath sounds on affected side, tracheal deviation away from affected side, and severe hypotension/JVD. Immediate emergency needle decompression with large-bore catheter (14-16G) at 2nd intercostal space midclavicular line or 4th/5th ICS anterior axillary line, followed by chest tube placement.
cheatSheet.clinicalRule: Do NOT wait for a chest X-ray to confirm if clinical signs of tension pneumothorax with hemodynamic instability are present.
cheatSheet.nclexAlert: Tracheal deviation is a late, definitive sign of mediastinal shift indicating immediate fatal shock.
examples: Mechanically ventilated ARDS client with sudden peak pressure alarm, drop in SpO2 to 78%, absent right breath sounds, and BP 70/40
cheatSheet.keyTakeaway: Immediate needle thoracostomy; never delay for diagnostic imaging.

cheatSheet.title: Cushing’s Triad (Increased ICP)
cheatSheet.meaning: Classic physiological response to critically increased intracranial pressure indicating impending brain herniation through foramen magnum.
cheatSheet.detailedUsage: Identify the triad: 1) Severe progressive hypertension with widening pulse pressure (elevated systolic with stable/dropped diastolic), 2) Bradycardia, 3) Irregular, Cheyne-Stokes respirations. Interventions: Elevate HOB 30 degrees, maintain neutral head/neck alignment, administer IV Mannitol or 3% hypertonic saline, avoid hip flexion, avoid clustering nursing activities.
cheatSheet.clinicalRule: Cushing’s Triad is the direct opposite of Hypovolemic Shock (which has tachycardia and narrowing pulse pressure).
cheatSheet.nclexAlert: Do NOT administer hypotonic solutions (like 0.45% NS or D5W) in increased ICP as they cause cerebral edema and brain death.
examples: Head trauma patient whose BP changes from 124/80 (pulse pressure 44) to 186/68 (pulse pressure 118) and HR slows from 88 to 46 bpm
cheatSheet.keyTakeaway: Widened pulse pressure + Bradycardia + Irregular respirations = Impending brain herniation.

cheatSheet.title: Cardiac Tamponade (Beck’s Triad)
cheatSheet.meaning: Excess fluid accumulation in pericardial sac compressing heart chambers and preventing ventricular filling.
cheatSheet.detailedUsage: Assess for Beck’s Triad: 1) Distended jugular veins (JVD), 2) Muffled/distant heart sounds, 3) Hypotension. Also assess for Pulsus Paradoxus (systolic drop >10 mmHg on inspiration). Prepare for emergency pericardiocentesis.
cheatSheet.clinicalRule: Pericardiocentesis restores cardiac output immediately by decompressing the pericardial space.
cheatSheet.nclexAlert: In post-cardiac surgery or pericarditis, sudden drop in chest tube drainage accompanied by JVD and hypotension strongly suggests cardiac tamponade.
examples: Client recovering from open-heart CABG suddenly has chest tube drainage drop from 100 mL/hr to 0, followed by BP 82/50, HR 124, and muffled S1/S2
cheatSheet.keyTakeaway: Muffled heart sounds + JVD + Hypotension = Emergency Pericardiocentesis.

cheatSheet.title: Hyperkalemia & Cardiac Arrest Protocol
cheatSheet.meaning: Serum potassium > 5.0 mEq/L, critical at > 6.0 mEq/L, threatening lethal ventricular arrhythmias (VFib / asystole).
cheatSheet.detailedUsage: Order of interventions: 1) IV Calcium Gluconate immediately (stabilizes cardiac membrane and prevents lethal arrhythmia), 2) IV Regular Insulin + 50% Dextrose (shifts potassium intracellularly), 3) Inhaled Albuterol high-dose, 4) Sodium Bicarbonate if acidotic, 5) Sodium Polystyrene Sulfonate (Kayexalate) or Patiromer or emergent Hemodialysis for permanent removal.
cheatSheet.clinicalRule: Calcium gluconate does NOT lower potassium levels; it only protects the heart while other meds shift or remove potassium.
cheatSheet.nclexAlert: Tall, peaked T waves and widened QRS complexes on ECG are warning signs of imminent ventricular fibrillation.
examples: End-stage renal disease patient with K+ 7.2 mEq/L and tall peaked T waves on telemetry
cheatSheet.keyTakeaway: Calcium gluconate first to protect myocardium, then insulin+D50 to shift K+ into cells.

cheatSheet.title: Ventricular Fibrillation & Pulseless V-Tach
cheatSheet.meaning: Lethal disorganized electrical rhythms without effective cardiac mechanical contraction resulting in zero cardiac output.
cheatSheet.detailedUsage: Call Code Blue immediately. Begin CPR (30 compressions : 2 breaths or continuous compressions with advanced airway). Defibrillate immediately with unsynchronized shock (120-200J biphasic or 360J monophasic). Resume CPR immediately after shock for 2 minutes before rhythm check. Administer IV Epinephrine 1 mg every 3-5 mins; Amiodarone 300 mg IV first bolus, 150 mg second bolus.
cheatSheet.clinicalRule: "V-Fib = D-Fib" (Defibrillate immediately). Synchronized cardioversion is strictly for clients WITH a pulse.
cheatSheet.nclexAlert: Never perform synchronized cardioversion on V-Fib; the machine will not find an R wave and will refuse to discharge.
examples: Unresponsive client showing chaotic baseline on telemetry without identifiable P waves or QRS complexes
cheatSheet.keyTakeaway: Immediate defibrillation followed by 2 minutes of uninterrupted CPR.

cheatSheet.title: Status Asthmaticus & Silent Chest Phenomenon
cheatSheet.meaning: Severe acute asthma exacerbation unresponsive to standard initial bronchodilator therapy, leading to dynamic hyperinflation and respiratory muscle exhaustion.
cheatSheet.detailedUsage: Continuous high-dose nebulized albuterol + ipratropium bromide, IV systemic corticosteroids (methylprednisolone), IV magnesium sulfate infusion (relaxes bronchial smooth muscle), and 100% humidified oxygen via non-rebreather mask.
cheatSheet.clinicalRule: A client with asthma who was previously wheezing loudly and suddenly becomes quiet ("silent chest") is NOT improving; they have stopped moving air.
cheatSheet.nclexAlert: Normalizing or elevated PaCO2 (>40 mmHg) in an asthma patient with tachypnea signifies impending respiratory failure and muscle exhaustion.
examples: Asthmatic child breathing 44/min who suddenly stops wheezing, becomes lethargic, and has SpO2 84%
cheatSheet.keyTakeaway: Loss of wheezing + lethargy in asthma = Emergency intubation.

cheatSheet.title: Compartment Syndrome (The 6 P’s)
cheatSheet.meaning: Elevated pressure within a confined osteofascial compartment compromising neurovascular perfusion and tissue viability.
cheatSheet.detailedUsage: Assess 6 P’s: Pain (early, out of proportion, unrelieved by opioids), Paresthesia (early numbness/tingling), Pallor, Poikilothermia, Pulselessness (late), Paralysis (late). Actions: Loosen tight casts or dressings, keep extremity AT HEART LEVEL (do NOT elevate above heart as it decreases arterial inflow), notify surgeon immediately for emergent fasciotomy.
cheatSheet.clinicalRule: Never elevate an extremity with suspected compartment syndrome above heart level; never apply ice.
cheatSheet.nclexAlert: Unrelieved deep severe pain that increases with passive dorsiflexion of toes/fingers is the earliest and most reliable hallmark.
examples: Tibial fracture client with cast reporting excruciating deep calf pain 30 minutes after IV morphine with tingling in toes
cheatSheet.keyTakeaway: Severe pain with passive stretch -> loosen cast -> keep level with heart -> call surgeon for fasciotomy.

cheatSheet.title: Lab Value: Serum Potassium (K+)
cheatSheet.meaning: Normal reference range: 3.5 - 5.0 mEq/L. Essential diagnostic indicator of organ function and homeostasis.
cheatSheet.detailedUsage: Regularly assess in client morning labs. Notify provider of critical outliers. Correlate with clinical presentation (e.g. ECG changes with electrolytes, bleeding signs with platelets).
cheatSheet.clinicalRule: Critical < 2.5 or > 6.0 mEq/L. Heart is sensitive: peaked T waves with high K+, U-waves with low K+.
cheatSheet.nclexAlert: Memorize this exact threshold: 3.5 - 5.0 mEq/L. Abnormal values appear constantly across med-surg prioritization.
examples: Client with Serum Potassium (K+) outside reference range requiring immediate IV correction or medication dose hold
cheatSheet.keyTakeaway: Serum Potassium (K+): 3.5 - 5.0 mEq/L. Critical for patient safety.

cheatSheet.title: Lab Value: Serum Sodium (Na+)
cheatSheet.meaning: Normal reference range: 135 - 145 mEq/L. Essential diagnostic indicator of organ function and homeostasis.
cheatSheet.detailedUsage: Regularly assess in client morning labs. Notify provider of critical outliers. Correlate with clinical presentation (e.g. ECG changes with electrolytes, bleeding signs with platelets).
cheatSheet.clinicalRule: Critical < 120 or > 160 mEq/L. Major regulator of neurological volume; hyponatremia causes cerebral edema and seizures.
cheatSheet.nclexAlert: Memorize this exact threshold: 135 - 145 mEq/L. Abnormal values appear constantly across med-surg prioritization.
examples: Client with Serum Sodium (Na+) outside reference range requiring immediate IV correction or medication dose hold
cheatSheet.keyTakeaway: Serum Sodium (Na+): 135 - 145 mEq/L. Critical for patient safety.

cheatSheet.title: Lab Value: Serum Calcium (Ca2+)
cheatSheet.meaning: Normal reference range: 8.5 - 10.5 mg/dL. Essential diagnostic indicator of organ function and homeostasis.
cheatSheet.detailedUsage: Regularly assess in client morning labs. Notify provider of critical outliers. Correlate with clinical presentation (e.g. ECG changes with electrolytes, bleeding signs with platelets).
cheatSheet.clinicalRule: Hypocalcemia causes tetany, Chvostek and Trousseau signs, prolonged QT interval.
cheatSheet.nclexAlert: Memorize this exact threshold: 8.5 - 10.5 mg/dL. Abnormal values appear constantly across med-surg prioritization.
examples: Client with Serum Calcium (Ca2+) outside reference range requiring immediate IV correction or medication dose hold
cheatSheet.keyTakeaway: Serum Calcium (Ca2+): 8.5 - 10.5 mg/dL. Critical for patient safety.

cheatSheet.title: Lab Value: Serum Magnesium (Mg2+)
cheatSheet.meaning: Normal reference range: 1.5 - 2.5 mEq/L. Essential diagnostic indicator of organ function and homeostasis.
cheatSheet.detailedUsage: Regularly assess in client morning labs. Notify provider of critical outliers. Correlate with clinical presentation (e.g. ECG changes with electrolytes, bleeding signs with platelets).
cheatSheet.clinicalRule: Critical for neuromuscular stability; low Mg causes Torsades de Pointes; high Mg causes loss of DTRs and respiratory depression.
cheatSheet.nclexAlert: Memorize this exact threshold: 1.5 - 2.5 mEq/L. Abnormal values appear constantly across med-surg prioritization.
examples: Client with Serum Magnesium (Mg2+) outside reference range requiring immediate IV correction or medication dose hold
cheatSheet.keyTakeaway: Serum Magnesium (Mg2+): 1.5 - 2.5 mEq/L. Critical for patient safety.

cheatSheet.title: Lab Value: Serum Chloride (Cl-)
cheatSheet.meaning: Normal reference range: 96 - 106 mEq/L. Essential diagnostic indicator of organ function and homeostasis.
cheatSheet.detailedUsage: Regularly assess in client morning labs. Notify provider of critical outliers. Correlate with clinical presentation (e.g. ECG changes with electrolytes, bleeding signs with platelets).
cheatSheet.clinicalRule: Follows sodium and maintains acid-base osmotic balance.
cheatSheet.nclexAlert: Memorize this exact threshold: 96 - 106 mEq/L. Abnormal values appear constantly across med-surg prioritization.
examples: Client with Serum Chloride (Cl-) outside reference range requiring immediate IV correction or medication dose hold
cheatSheet.keyTakeaway: Serum Chloride (Cl-): 96 - 106 mEq/L. Critical for patient safety.

cheatSheet.title: Lab Value: Serum Phosphorus (PO4 3-)
cheatSheet.meaning: Normal reference range: 2.5 - 4.5 mg/dL. Essential diagnostic indicator of organ function and homeostasis.
cheatSheet.detailedUsage: Regularly assess in client morning labs. Notify provider of critical outliers. Correlate with clinical presentation (e.g. ECG changes with electrolytes, bleeding signs with platelets).
cheatSheet.clinicalRule: Inversely related to calcium; high in chronic kidney failure, low in refeeding syndrome.
cheatSheet.nclexAlert: Memorize this exact threshold: 2.5 - 4.5 mg/dL. Abnormal values appear constantly across med-surg prioritization.
examples: Client with Serum Phosphorus (PO4 3-) outside reference range requiring immediate IV correction or medication dose hold
cheatSheet.keyTakeaway: Serum Phosphorus (PO4 3-): 2.5 - 4.5 mg/dL. Critical for patient safety.

cheatSheet.title: Lab Value: Blood Urea Nitrogen (BUN)
cheatSheet.meaning: Normal reference range: 7 - 20 mg/dL. Essential diagnostic indicator of organ function and homeostasis.
cheatSheet.detailedUsage: Regularly assess in client morning labs. Notify provider of critical outliers. Correlate with clinical presentation (e.g. ECG changes with electrolytes, bleeding signs with platelets).
cheatSheet.clinicalRule: Elevated in dehydration (prerenal azotemia), high protein intake, or renal insufficiency.
cheatSheet.nclexAlert: Memorize this exact threshold: 7 - 20 mg/dL. Abnormal values appear constantly across med-surg prioritization.
examples: Client with Blood Urea Nitrogen (BUN) outside reference range requiring immediate IV correction or medication dose hold
cheatSheet.keyTakeaway: Blood Urea Nitrogen (BUN): 7 - 20 mg/dL. Critical for patient safety.

cheatSheet.title: Lab Value: Serum Creatinine
cheatSheet.meaning: Normal reference range: 0.6 - 1.2 mg/dL. Essential diagnostic indicator of organ function and homeostasis.
cheatSheet.detailedUsage: Regularly assess in client morning labs. Notify provider of critical outliers. Correlate with clinical presentation (e.g. ECG changes with electrolytes, bleeding signs with platelets).
cheatSheet.clinicalRule: Best indicator of kidney function; constant daily production from muscle metabolism.
cheatSheet.nclexAlert: Memorize this exact threshold: 0.6 - 1.2 mg/dL. Abnormal values appear constantly across med-surg prioritization.
examples: Client with Serum Creatinine outside reference range requiring immediate IV correction or medication dose hold
cheatSheet.keyTakeaway: Serum Creatinine: 0.6 - 1.2 mg/dL. Critical for patient safety.
